results.summary: Every Boolean algebra $B$ embeds in a power set algebra: there are a set $X$ and an injective map $f$ from $B$ to the power set of $X$ such that $f(a \sqcup b) = f(a) \cup f(b)$ and $f(a \sqcap b) = f(a) \cap f(b)$ for all $a, b \in B$, $f(\top) = X$ and $f(\bot) = \emptyset$.

results.title: Farey series over a field

results.summary: Let $F$ be a field and $n$ a natural number. results.title: Resource-allocation snapshot
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A resource-allocation snapshot, for a type $P$ of processes and a type $R$ of resources, records for each resource the process holding it, if any (so each resource has at most one holder), and for each process $p$ and resource $r$ whether $p$ has an outstanding request for $r$. A process never requests a resource it holds.

results.title: Wait-for relation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In a resource-allocation snapshot $s$, a process $p$ waits for a process $q$ when there is a resource $r$ that $p$ requests in $s$ and that $q$ holds in $s$.

results.title: Deadlocked set of processes
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In a resource-allocation snapshot $s$, a set $D$ of processes is deadlocked when $D$ is nonempty and every process $p \in D$ waits in $s$ for some process $q \in D$, that is, $p$ requests in $s$ a resource that $q$ holds in $s$.

results.title: Circular wait
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A resource-allocation snapshot $s$ has circular wait when some process $p$ waits for itself through a chain of one or more wait-for edges in $s$, that is, there are processes $p = p_0, p_1, \dots, p_k = p$ with $k \ge 1$ such that $p_{i-1}$ waits for $p_i$ in $s$ for each $1 \le i \le k$.

results.title: No process waits for itself directly
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a resource-allocation snapshot, no process $p$ waits for itself, that is, there is no resource that $p$ both requests and holds.

results.title: A process whose requests are all free waits for no one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a resource-allocation snapshot, if no resource requested by a process $p$ has a holder, then $p$ waits for no process $q$.

results.title: Circular wait yields a deadlocked set
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a resource-allocation snapshot has circular wait, that is, some process $p$ waits for itself through a chain of one or more wait-for edges, then some set of processes is deadlocked.

results.title: A deadlocked set forces circular wait
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a resource-allocation snapshot with finitely many processes, if some set of processes is deadlocked, then the snapshot has circular wait: some process waits for itself through a chain of one or more wait-for edges.

results.title: Deadlock is circular wait
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a resource-allocation snapshot with finitely many processes, some set of processes is deadlocked if and only if the snapshot has circular wait, that is, some process waits for itself through a chain of one or more wait-for edges.

results.title: Havender's resource ordering
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $s$ be a resource-allocation snapshot and let $\mathrm{rank}$ assign a natural number to each resource. The snapshot $s$ is ordered by $\mathrm{rank}$ when, for every process $p$, every resource $r$ that $p$ requests in $s$ and every resource $r'$ that $p$ holds in $s$, we have $\mathrm{rank}(r') < \mathrm{rank}(r)$: each process requests only resources ranked strictly above every resource it holds.

results.title: Resource ordering prevents circular wait
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mathrm{rank}$ assign a natural number to each resource. If a resource-allocation snapshot is ordered by $\mathrm{rank}$ (Havender's discipline), that is, $\mathrm{rank}(r') < \mathrm{rank}(r)$ whenever some process requests $r$ and holds $r'$, then the snapshot has no circular wait: no process waits for itself through a chain of one or more wait-for edges.

results.title: Resource ordering prevents deadlock
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mathrm{rank}$ assign a natural number to each resource. If a resource-allocation snapshot with finitely many processes is ordered by $\mathrm{rank}$ (Havender's discipline), that is, $\mathrm{rank}(r') < \mathrm{rank}(r)$ whenever some process requests $r$ and holds $r'$, then no set of processes is deadlocked.
